newsitem.title: GREECE: Greek government makes small gesture to farmers.
newsitem.headline: Greek government makes small gesture to farmers.

text.p: Greece's government made a small gesture on Wednesday towards farmers who have blockaded roads for 21 days but appeared determined to reject any significant concessions as the number of barricades dwindled.
Agriculture minister Stephanos Tzoumakas said the European Union had agreed to allow Greece to divert some agricultural development funds towards paying for crops damaged by weather.

That was not among the main demands of the farmers but would be welcome news for many hard hit by recent storms. Cotton farmers in the central Thessaly region and northern Thrace have lost crops and complained compensation was too small.
Farmers, who are demanding cheaper fuel and equipment and higher state subsidies on their products, showed some signs of fatigue, with the nearest blockade to Athens being lifted.

But although the number of barricades was dwindling, farmers vowed to march on Athens for a rally on Thursday to push for a meeting with Prime Minister Costas Simitis, who has refused to meet them until they abandon their blockade.
"Shouting against the EU does not help the country's agricultural economy. We need deep reforms that are long overdue," Tzoumakas told a news conference.
He said he would cooperate with the National Economy ministry to ask the EU to pay about 10 billion drachmas ($40 million) in compensation.
National Economy Minister Yannos Papandoniou also appeared adamant on refusing all demands.
"As far as the government is concerned our position is very clear. We shall not give in. There is no room for further concessions to farmers," he told Reuters Television.
His tough 1997 budget has angered workers by clamping down on state hiring, limiting wage rises for another year, levying new taxes and eliminating hundreds of tax breaks.
Simitis says the strict budget is essential to meet economic targets so Greece can join a single European currency by the year 2001.
Continuing strikes by seamen have left ships docked at ports around Greece. State doctors, tax, customs and finance ministry employees also went on strike on Wednesday.
Civil aviation unions, except air traffic controllers, have annnounced a 24-hour strike on Friday that is sure to disrupt flight schedules.

Government officials said a walkout by doctors, civil servants, diplomats and seamen on Tuesday, the opening of the five-day debate in parliament on the 1997 austerity budget, caused minimal disruption.
But the seamens' walkout, in its second day, halted commercial transport and tourist ferries.
